verdict.reasoning: All three provisions describe the same biennial report by the Administrator to the Senate and House Small Business Committees on the status of the nationwide campaign. Provision [1] is the parent subsection containing the report paragraph, [2] is that paragraph, and [3] is the 'in general' subparagraph; the contents subparagraph merely specifies what the single report must include. The recurring deadline is part of the same duty.

Both provisions state the same single reporting duty: the Secretary's annual report to the Veterans' Affairs Committees on the long-term TBI rehabilitation program. Provision [2] is simply subsection (d) of the full section in [1], and the enumerated items (1)-(3) are required contents of that one report, not separate duties. The remaining subsections impose no reporting obligation to Congress.

All three provisions are nested versions of the same text: the full section, subsection (d), and paragraph (d)(3). The only duty to Congress is the Director's annual report to the House Financial Services and Senate Banking Committees describing actions taken to eliminate interest rate disparities. The other provisions (housing goals, timing, transition, data submission to the Director) impose no reporting duty to Congress. Therefore one distinct duty.

Both provisions state the same duty: the Deputy Attorney General's annual report to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees on approved conference expenditures. Provision [1] is the parent paragraph containing subparagraph (C), and [2] is that subparagraph quoted alone. The limitation and written-approval subparagraphs impose no reporting duty to Congress. Therefore there is one distinct duty.

All five provisions state the same single annual report: the Secretary of Defense's report to the congressional defense committees on the status of prepositioned materiel, due by the date of the President's budget request. Items (1), (2), (3), and (12) are merely required contents of that one report, each quoted along with the same parent lead-in. A report plus its content list counts as one duty, so there is exactly one distinct reporting duty.

All five provisions describe the same single annual report under § 360e–1(a)(3): the Secretary's report to the Senate HELP Committee and House Energy and Commerce Committee, due 18 months after September 27, 2007, and annually thereafter. The excerpts are nested versions of the same duty—the parent section, subsection (a), paragraph (3), and individual content subparagraphs (A) and (B), which are merely required contents of that one report. The application-information requirements in (a)(1)-(2) run to the Secretary, not Congress, so they add nothing.

All five provisions restate the same single duty: the Secretary's annual written report to specified House and Senate committees on emergency response and preparedness under subsection (d). Items (1)-(4) are merely required contents of that one report, and the subdivision-level excerpts repeat the same parent duty. Subsections (a)-(c) impose no reporting duty to Congress.
All five provisions describe the same single annual report by the Senior Advisor under subsection (e); items (1)-(5) are merely required contents repeated in subdivisions, so they count as one duty.

Both provisions state the same annual report: subsection (d) requires the President to submit a report to Congress by February 1 each year on activities under the section. Provision [1] is the full section containing that same subsection, so it adds no additional congressional reporting duty. Therefore there is one distinct duty.

Provision [2] is simply subsection (c) restated, so it adds nothing new. Within the full section: (a) requires publication on a public website, not a submission to Congress, so it contributes no congressional duty by itself. (b) is a distinct duty: a classified list of non-complying countries provided to the appropriate congressional committees. (c) is a distinct duty: an annual classified update on U.S. anti-corruption efforts, different subject and format. (d)(1) merely sets deadlines/recurrence for the duties in (a)-(c) and is not separate. (d)(2) is a distinct duty: a one-time report on methodology and proposed budget, with its own deadline and subject. (e) imposes a distinct conditional submission to the committees of classified country information plus a national-interest justification when countries are withheld from the public list. Total: 4 distinct duties.

All four provisions state the same single annual report by the Council to the specified committees; items (1), (2), and (5) are merely required contents of that report repeated with the parent lead-in. Therefore only one distinct reporting duty.

All three provisions are nested versions of the same annual report: the Secretary's report to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and Senate Environment and Public Works Committee describing ability-to-pay determinations. Provision [1] is the full subsection containing the report paragraph, [2] is that paragraph, and [3] is the 'in general' subparagraph stating the duty; the contents list and the chief's report permission are part of the same duty, not separate ones. Hence one distinct duty.

All four provisions state the same single reporting duty: the Secretary of the Treasury's written report to the named House and Senate committees assessing the likelihood of full repayment, due within 30 days of Board approval and annually thereafter. The paragraphs (b)(1)-(3) merely list required contents of that one report, and the initial deadline plus annual recurrence count as one duty. Subsection (a) imposes instruction/voting duties, not reports to Congress.

Both excerpts cover the same provision: the requirement that budget justification documents submitted to Congress with the President's budget set forth specified information on aviation bonuses. The second excerpt is simply the subparagraph (B) already contained within the first. Subparagraph (A) imposes an analytic duty on the Secretary but no submission to Congress. Thus there is one distinct congressional reporting duty, with clauses (i)-(iv) being its required contents.

Both provisions state the same single reporting duty: the President's annual report on Russian Federation funds intended to influence elections in Europe and Eurasia. Provision [2] is simply subsection (a) of the full section in [1]; the form-of-report and definitions subsections add no separate duty.

All five provisions describe the same annual report by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue under section 6307(c), due each March to the Senate Finance/Appropriations and House Ways and Means/Appropriations Committees. Paragraphs (1)-(3) merely enumerate required contents (prior, current, and following fiscal year data) of that single report, and the section-level and subsection-level excerpts repeat the same duty. Therefore only one distinct congressional reporting duty exists.

All three provisions are nested versions of the same text, each containing the single annual report to Congress under clause (iii) — the Administrator's annual report to the Senate EPW and House Energy and Commerce committees describing enforcement actions. The broader provisions merely repeat the parent context; the state notification in clause (ii) is to the State, not Congress, so it contributes zero. Total: one distinct duty.

All five provisions come from the same section and describe the same biennial joint report by the Administrator and Under Secretary on the condition of the Nation's coastal ecosystems. Items (3)-(6) are merely content elements of that single report, repeated with the parent lead-in, so they do not create additional duties.

Both excerpts describe the same annual report by the Administrator on the Initiative to the House Transportation and Infrastructure and Senate Commerce Committees; provision [2] is simply the parent paragraph repeated. The stakeholder comments requirement in paragraph (2) is an appendix to that same report, not an independent submission. Therefore there is one distinct congressional reporting duty.

Both provisions describe the same duty: the Secretary of Energy's annual submission to Congress of a future-years energy program. The second excerpt is just subsection (a) of the first. Subsection (b) lists required contents of that same submission, and subsection (c) is a budgeting consistency requirement, not a separate report. Therefore there is one distinct reporting duty.

Both provisions state the same annual report by the Director to the Secretary of Agriculture and the House and Senate Agriculture Committees; provision [2] is merely a subdivision listing one of the required contents of that single report. Contents lists and parent/subdivision repetition count as one duty.

All four provisions are nested versions of the same text, with the only congressional reporting duty being the accountability mechanism's annual report to the Board and appropriate congressional committees on compliance with best practices/standards and complaint resolution (subsection (b)(2)(A)). The broader excerpts simply restate that duty within parent provisions; other parts (safeguards, ombudsman, annual internal review) impose no duty to report to Congress."}

All three provisions describe contents of the single annual report to Congress under § 2282d. [1] is the parent subparagraph containing [2] and [3]; [2] requires inclusion of proposed modifications in the annual report and [3] specifies what must accompany each such modification. These are content requirements of one recurring annual report, not separate submissions, so they count as a single distinct duty.

All four provisions state the same single annual report by the United States Advisory Council on Human Trafficking under subsection (e), containing findings from the reviews under (d)(2). The subdivisions merely list the recipients (Task Force chair, Group members, House committees, Senate committees), and the excerpts repeat the same lead-in text. Multiple recipients of one report do not create separate duties, and the first deadline plus annual recurrence is one duty.

Both provisions are subparagraphs of the same single reporting requirement: the Secretary of State's report to the appropriate congressional committees containing the designated persons list. Subparagraphs (A) and (C) merely enumerate required contents of that one report, so they constitute one distinct duty.

Both provisions describe the same annual joint report to the congressional intelligence committees on foreign commercial providers and procured cyber vulnerabilities. Provision [2] is simply subsection (a) of the full section in [1]; the elements, form, and definitions subsections merely elaborate on that single report. Therefore only one distinct reporting duty exists.

Provisions [2]-[5] all restate the same single duty: the President's annual Report on Small Business and Competition due by January 20, with (a)(1)-(5) merely listing its required contents. Provision [1] contains that same report plus subsection (b), which requires the President to transmit simultaneously an appendix report, by agency and department, on the dollar value of Federal contracts and awards to small, minority-, female-, and veteran-owned businesses \u2014 a different subject and a separately mandated submission, so it counts as a second duty. Subsection (c) supplementary reports are discretionary ('may') and derivative of the main report, and (d) merely directs committee referral, so neither adds a distinct duty.

Provision [1] contains two duties: (1) an annual report to eight listed committees on activities and agreements under the section, and (2) a separate advance notification, at least 15 days before entering into a fee agreement, to the members of Congress representing the affected State or district. These have different subjects, triggers, and deadlines, so they are separate. Provision [2] is simply the first of those duties repeated as a subdivision, adding nothing new. Total distinct duties: 2.
All four provisions describe the same annual report by the Secretary under § 24911(j); paragraphs (1)-(3) merely enumerate required contents of that single report, so they count as one duty.

Both provisions describe the same submission: the Secretary of State's plan setting forth a National Security Assistance Strategy to the appropriate committees of Congress. Provision [2] is simply subsection (a) of the full section in [1]. Subsections (b) and (c) merely specify the required elements and coverage of that same plan, and the '180 days...and annually thereafter' language is a first deadline plus recurrence of one duty, not separate duties.

Total: 1 distinct duty.

Both provisions state the same single duty: the Secretary of Defense's annual March 15 report on the School's activities and operating costs. Provision [1] is the full section containing subsection (f), and provision [2] is that same subsection quoted alone. No other congressional reporting duty appears in the section.

Provision [1] contains two separate informing duties: paragraph (c)(1) requires the Secretary of State to regularly provide the appropriate congressional committees a list of units prohibited from receiving assistance, and paragraph (c)(2) requires the Secretary to inform the committees whenever the recipient government withholds assistance from a unit. These have different triggers and subjects, so they are separate duties. Provision [2] is simply the text of (c)(1) standing alone, duplicating the first duty and adding nothing new. Total distinct duties: 2.

All three provisions describe the same annual report under subsection (c) by the Secretary of State, in coordination with the Secretary of Commerce, on Taiwan's meaningful participation in ICAO. Items [2] and [3] are merely the required contents (paragraphs (2) and (3)) of that single report, repeated with the parent lead-in. A report plus its required contents counts as one duty.

Both provisions state the same single duty: the Secretary of State shall keep Congress fully and currently informed with respect to leases or rental arrangements approved under the section. Provision [2] is simply subsection (a) of the full section quoted in [1], so it repeats rather than adds a duty. Subsection (b) on advance payments imposes no reporting duty to Congress.

All five provisions describe the same single CBO report under subsection (b), with the numbered paragraphs merely listing required contents. The parent provision states the duty and the subdivisions repeat it, so they count as one distinct reporting duty.

All four provisions are nested versions of the same single reporting requirement in subsection (b): the President's annual report to the appropriate congressional committees on executive branch actions under the subchapter and related national emergency. The subparagraphs (A)-(F) are merely required contents, and paragraph (2) only specifies the form (unclassified with classified annex), not a separate submission. Therefore there is one distinct duty.

Provision [2] is wholly contained within provision [1], so it adds nothing new. Within [1], the annual budget prepared by the Commissioner and submitted by the President to Congress (b)(1)(A), together with the required itemization of anti-fraud funding (b)(1)(B), is a single submission plus its required contents \u2014 one duty. Paragraph (b)(3) requires a separate report, covering a different subject (expenditures of section 901(b)(2)(B) funds, with its own itemized contents) and its own coverage period (fiscal years 2016\u20132021), even though it is transmitted with the budget; that is a second distinct duty. Paragraph (b)(2) states no reporting duty to Congress.

All five provisions concern the same single annual report by the Comptroller General to the congressional intelligence committees on cybersecurity and surveillance threats to Congress. Subsection (a) states the duty and deadline/recurrence; (b) lists required contents; (c) prescribes consultation; (d) prescribes form. These are components of one duty, and the full-section text is a repetition of the same duty.

Provision [2] is simply paragraph (b)(5) quoted in full within provision [1]. The only duty to Congress in either text is the annual report by the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, due by March 31 each year, on the effectiveness of visa systems and anti-circumvention measures. The other paragraphs (customs procedures, certificates of origin, penalties, transshipment definition) impose no congressional reporting duty. Therefore the two provisions together state one distinct duty.

All three provisions describe the same single annual report by the Secretary on the impact of transfers on immigration functions. Provision [2] is subsection (a) containing the duty plus its required contents, and [3] is the parent duty statement repeated at the paragraph level. The contents list (A)-(H) is part of the same report, and the sense-of-Congress subsection (b) states no reporting duty. Therefore, one distinct duty.

All three provisions describe the same annual written report from the Secretary to the Senate Environment and Public Works and House Transportation and Infrastructure Committees. Provision [2] is the parent duty, [3] is one of its required contents, and [1] adds a comment opportunity to Cooperative Committee members (not a duty to Congress) whose comments are folded into the same report. Therefore one distinct congressional reporting duty.

Both provisions state the same duty: the Director of DIA's annual written analysis of exit survey/interview results submitted to the appropriate congressional committees. Provision [1] is the parent subsection containing paragraph (2), and [2] is that same paragraph quoted alone. The exit survey requirement in (c)(1) is an internal agency duty, not a report to Congress, and its results are folded into the single annual submission. Therefore only one distinct reporting duty exists.

All four provisions describe the same annual report by the operational energy working group to the congressional defense committees due February 1 each year. Items [2]-[4] are the parent subparagraph and its content subdivisions, and subparagraph (B) merely specifies form (unclassified with classified annex). Contents lists and form requirements do not create separate duties, so there is one distinct reporting duty.

All four provisions describe the same single obligation: the Secretary's biennial written report to the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance Committees under subsection (c). Paragraphs (1) and (2) merely specify the required contents of that one report, and provision [1] is the full section text containing the same duty plus non-reporting requirements (technical assistance plan, interagency coordination) that impose no separate duty to Congress.

Both provisions state the same duty: the Secretary of Energy must notify the appropriate congressional committees of the determination of critical civil nuclear technologies, within 90 days and every five years thereafter. Provision [2] is simply subparagraph (B) of the parent provision quoted in [1], so the notification duty is counted once, with its recurrence treated as part of the single duty.

Both provisions state the same single duty: the Chief Administrative Officer's semiannual itemized report of House disbursements. Provision [2] is just subsection (a) of the full section in [1]; the remaining subsections specify contents, printing, exclusions, and effective date, which are part of the same duty rather than separate submissions.

All five provisions describe the same annual report under §2519(c): the same Secretary, same committees, same deadline (May 31, 2026, annually for 5 years). Items (1), (3), (4), and (6) are merely required contents of that single report, and the parent provision states the duty. Content lists and repetition in subdivisions count as one duty.

Both provisions describe the same annual report by the Secretary of Defense to the congressional defense committees under subsection (g); the second is merely a content element (paragraph (3)) of that same report. A report and its required contents count as one duty.

Provision [2] is simply subsection (d) of the full section given in [1]. The only duty to Congress stated is the Secretary's quarterly briefing to the congressional defense committees on military cyber activities or operations (folded into the section 484 quarterly briefing). The other subsections state authorities, affirmations, rules of construction, and definitions, with no separate reporting duty (the reference to section 395 reporting is a cross-reference, not a duty imposed here). Both passages describe the same single briefing obligation, so they state one distinct duty.

All three provisions are nested versions of the same requirement: the Secretary's annual report to the House Agriculture and Education and Labor Committees and the Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee describing the status of State demonstration projects and evaluation results. The parent provision adds assessment and evaluation mandates, but those are not separate duties to Congress; the recurring deadline is part of the single duty.

All five provisions state the same single annual reporting duty: the Secretary's annual report to the Veterans' Affairs Committees on the operation of the high technology program. Items (1), (2), (3), and (5) are merely required contents of that one report, repeated alongside the parent lead-in. A report plus its list of required contents counts as one duty, so there is one distinct reporting duty.

All five provisions describe the same biennial report under §247b–4(c): same Secretary, same deadline (February 1 of fiscal year 1999 and every second year thereafter), same committees. The paragraphs (1), (2), (3), and (5) are merely required contents of that single report, repeated with the parent lead-in. Therefore they collectively state one distinct reporting duty.

All five provisions concern the same section. The only duty to Congress is the biennial report by the Secretary, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense, under subsection (e)(2); items (C), (D), and (E) are merely required contents of that report, and the excerpts repeat it. The (e)(1) report by grant recipients goes to the Secretary and Secretary of Defense, not Congress, so it contributes zero. Hence one distinct congressional reporting duty.

All provisions concern the single annual report under subsection (b)(4) by the Attorney General, in consultation with the Secretary of State, to the named Judiciary and foreign affairs committees. Items [3]-[5] are just the content subparagraphs (A)-(C) of that same report, repeating the parent lead-in, and [1] states the substantive offense, penalties, and jurisdiction with no reporting duty. The first deadline plus annual recurrence counts as one duty.

Provision [1] is the full section, whose only congressional duty is subsection (b): the Commission must include in its annual reports to Congress plans and findings on implementing the section. Provision [2] is that same subsection (b) quoted alone. Subsection (a) merely directs establishment of research and information programs and states no reporting duty. Since the second excerpt duplicates the duty already stated in the first, there is one distinct reporting duty.

Provision [1] is the full section, whose only congressional reporting duty is subsection (c); provision [2] is that same subsection (c) quoted alone. Subsections (a) and (b) impose no reporting duty to Congress. The single annual report by the Secretary of the Treasury on implementation status, with its initial deadline and recurrence, counts as one duty.

Provision [2] merely repeats subsection (a) of the full section shown in [1], so it adds nothing new. Within the section, the Committee's annual report to the President and Congress is one duty; the deadline in (c) and the contents/assessment description are part of that same duty, and the open-ended 'such other reports as may be requested' is an adjunct of the same reporting obligation by the same entity. Subsection (b) imposes a separate duty on a different entity (the Secretary of Commerce) with its own independent 60-day deadline and distinct content (comments and recommendations), so it counts as a second distinct duty.

All five provisions describe the same annual report by the Social Media Working Group to the appropriate congressional committees; the subdivisions merely enumerate required contents of that single report. A report plus its contents list counts as one duty, so there is 1 distinct reporting duty.

Both excerpts cover the same material: provision [2] is just subsection (c) of provision [1]. The only duty to Congress is the President's certification to the appropriate congressional committees regarding assurances from a person employing North Korean labor, plus the 180-day recertification of those same conditions. The recertification is simply the recurrence of the initial certification on the same subject by the same reporting entity, so it counts as one duty rather than two. The sanctions designation and imposition provisions state no reporting duty to Congress.

Both provisions describe the same single implementation report by the Attorney General to Congress. Provision [1] is the parent subsection containing the duty plus its required contents and privacy limitation; provision [2] is the same duty restated from paragraph (1). The annual recurrence after the initial 2-year deadline is part of one duty.

Both provisions describe the same annual Home Heating Readiness Report submitted to Congress by the Secretary through the EIA Administrator. Provision [1] is the full section including the report's required contents and an information-request authority, while [2] is just the parent duty subsection. The contents list and information-gathering authority are part of the single report duty, not separate submissions.

Provision [2] is simply subsection (c) of the full section in [1]. The only duty to Congress is the annual funding estimate submitted with the President's budget request; the rest of the section (establishment of the office and its responsibilities) states no congressional reporting duty. The repeated subsection counts once.

All four provisions concern the same single requirement: the Secretary of State must include a separate section in the Annual Report identifying countries with a pattern of noncompliance. Provision [1] is the parent, [2] states the duty, and [3] and [4] merely specify required contents of that same section. Contents lists and subdivisions repeating a parent duty count as one duty.

Provision [1] contains two separate obligations: subsection (a) requires the President's annual budget submission to Congress to set forth, as a separate item, the amounts requested for all Department of Defense security cooperation programs (a distinct annual disclosure to Congress), and subsection (b) requires the Secretary to submit a semiannual report to the appropriate committees on the obligation and expenditure of security cooperation funds. Paragraphs (b)(1) and (b)(2) are merely the two recurring deadlines of that single semiannual report, not separate duties. Provision [2] is just a re-statement of subsection (b) and adds nothing new. Total distinct duties: the budget display requirement and the semiannual expenditure report = 2.

All four provisions are nested versions of the same text from 15 U.S.C. 644a. The only duty to Congress is the Council's annual report to the House and Senate Small Business Committees under subsection (b)(5), with subparagraphs (A)-(C) merely listing required contents. The other provisions (establishment, membership, meetings, etc.) state no congressional reporting duty.

Provision [2] is simply subsection (c) of the full section quoted in [1]. Both state the same single duty: the Secretary's annual report to the House and Senate Agriculture Committees on progress implementing the section. Subsections (a) and (b) impose data-collection and evaluation tasks but no separate submission to Congress, so they contribute zero.

All three provisions repeat the same parent duty: the Inspector General must report to Congress the results of each periodic audit of the Commercial Service. Paragraphs (1)-(3) merely enumerate required contents of that single audit report, so they constitute one distinct reporting duty.

Both provisions describe the same annual report on the financial impact study submitted by the Secretary of Agriculture to the House and Senate Agriculture Committees. Provision [2] is simply subsection (b) of the full section quoted in [1]. Subsection (a) states the study requirement (no separate congressional submission) and (c) limits use of the study, so neither adds a duty. One distinct reporting duty.

All five provisions describe the same annual report by the President to the appropriate congressional committees on sanctions imposed under section 10102. Provision [2] is the parent duty; [3] and [4] are merely required contents of that report; [5] is the recurrence/deadline for the same report; [1] is the whole section including the initial deadline, recurrence, and form requirements (including the 15-day advance notice before classified-annex listing, which is an ancillary condition of the same report). Therefore there is one distinct reporting duty.

Both excerpts address the same obligation: the information and data already required to be reported under subsection (a) must separately detail specified categories of small business concerns. Provision [1] is the parent lead-in with its list of categories, and [2] is simply paragraph (1) of that same list. A report plus the breakdown of contents it must include counts as one duty, and a duty repeated in its subdivisions is not multiplied. There is no separate subject, reporting entity, or independent deadline here, so the two provisions together state one distinct reporting duty to Congress.

All five excerpts describe the same reporting scheme in 6 U.S.C. 225(b)(4). Subparagraph (A) creates one duty: the Secretary of Homeland Security's report (due one year after Dec. 23, 2022, biennially thereafter) whose clauses (i) and (ii) are merely required contents, so excerpts [3], [4], [5] and the (A) portion of [1] and [2] all restate that single duty. Subparagraph (B) creates a second, separate duty: a Comptroller General (GAO) report with its own reporting entity, subject (evaluating the data collection and metrics), and independent deadline tied to each of the first three (A) reports. The program-establishment, considerations, and update paragraphs state no duty to Congress. Total: 2 distinct duties.

Both provisions describe the same quarterly briefing by the Assistant Secretary of Defense for SO/LIC to the congressional defense committees; the second is simply a content element (paragraph (1)) of that same briefing. A report and its required contents count as one duty.

All provisions restate the same single annual report by the Secretary of Labor to the Veterans' Affairs Committees, due February 1 each year. The paragraphs are merely the required contents of that one report, so they do not create separate duties.

Both provisions describe the same obligation: the Attorney General's semiannual briefing/report to the intelligence and judiciary committees on implementation of the subchapter. Provision [2] is simply subsection (a) of the full section in [1], and subsection (b) merely lists the required contents of that same report. A report plus its content list counts as one duty, so there is a single distinct congressional reporting duty.

Both provisions are subparagraphs of the same single reporting requirement in subsection (d): one semiannual report by the Secretary of the Treasury on Sudan's governance and fiscal transparency steps. Items (2) and (3) merely list required contents of that one report, so they constitute one distinct duty.

All five provisions come from subsection (k) of 
civil section 262a. Provisions [2]
dash[5] all state the same single duty: the Secretary's annual report to the Senate HELP and House Energy and Commerce Committees, with subparagraphs (A)-(C) merely listing required contents 
dash that is one duty. Provision [1] contains that same annual report plus a separate duty in paragraph (k)(1): notification to the same committees within 72 hours of a release, loss, or theft at a Federal laboratory facility, with a 14-day follow-up update on the same event (treated as part of the same notification duty, being a follow-up on the same subject/event). The truncated reference to paragraph (3) states no discernible duty. Total distinct duties: the incident notification and the annual report = 2.

[1] is an annual certification by the Secretary of Energy to the congressional defense committees regarding programs and budget meeting pit production requirements — one duty. [2] is a separate annual report by the NNSA Administrator on planned production goals of covered projects, with its own deadline and trigger; paragraph (2) merely lists its required contents, so it merges with paragraph (1). Different reporting entities, subjects, and deadlines make these two distinct duties.

Note [1] contains two separate duties: (a) a 15-day advance notification to the Appropriations Committees before operationalizing an unlicensed influx facility, with specified content, and (b) an independent report due within 60 days of bringing the facility online and monthly thereafter detailing children in care, lengths of stay, etc. These have different subjects, triggers, and deadlines. Note [2] states one duty: a report (due 14 days after enactment and monthly thereafter) on children separated from parents/guardians, with its listed contents counting as part of the single report. Total: 3 distinct duties.

Provision [1] is a fund-allocation rule describing permissible uses of fees and penalties; its mentions of reports under subsection (i) and annual reports under subsection (j)(4) are cross-references to duties imposed elsewhere, not independent statements of a reporting duty, so it contributes zero. Provision [2] imposes one duty: the Administrator's annual progress report to Congress (initial December 31, 1989 deadline plus recurrence counts as one), with subparagraphs (A)-(D) merely listing required contents and paragraph (2) governing referral to committees rather than creating a new report.

Provision (b)(14) directs the plan to include analysis yielding periodic recommendations to Congress, and subsection (e) requires the Task Force's annual report to the President and Congress to contain 'such recommendations as are developed under subsection (b)(14).' The annual report is the vehicle through which the (b)(14) recommendations reach Congress, so the two provisions describe a single congressional submission (a report plus its required contents), not two independent duties.

Provision [1] (§544) contains three congressional submissions: (d) transmittal to the appropriate committees of each annual mishandled-wheelchair report (the (c) evaluation/public website posting is the same report, so counted once with (d)); (e)(1) the strategic roadmap on in-cabin wheelchair restraint feasibility submitted to the committees; and (e)(3) the report on the results of the economic/financial feasibility study. Subsections (a), (b), (e)(2), and (f) impose rulemaking, refund, study, and definitional duties with no congressional submission, so they add nothing. Provision [2] (§545) states one duty: an annual report to the appropriate committees on disability-related aviation consumer complaints, with subsection (b) merely listing its required contents. Total: 3 + 1 = 4 distinct duties.

Provision (d) requires an annual report from the Secretary of Energy on compliance of covered foreign countries and end-users, with its enumerated contents counting as one duty. Provision (e) requires a separate report on Department of Energy review activities for transfers to all foreign countries, with a different subject and an independent deadline tied to the President's budget submission; its 'Elements' paragraph is merely the contents of that same report. Thus there are two distinct reporting duties.

Provision [1] (subparagraph (K)) contains two separate obligations: (i) a 30-day advance notification to the four named committees before carrying out a prize competition activity, and (ii) an annual report to those same committees on prize competition activities, with an enumerated list of required contents (the content list is part of the single report duty, not additional duties). Provision [2] is simply clause (i) standing alone, restating the same advance-notice duty already counted in [1], so it adds nothing new. Total distinct duties: the advance notice and the annual report = 2.

Provision [1] contains one duty to Congress: subparagraph (J)'s annual report to the Speaker of the House and President pro tempore of the Senate on the effectiveness of ombudsman services. The other listed functions (advocacy, recommendations to the Assistant Secretary, keeping the Secretary informed, standards-setting, and the published best-practices report in (M)) are not submissions to Congress. Provision [2] contains one duty to Congress: paragraph (7)'s report, due December 31, 2020 and annually thereafter, from the Center director to the Secretary and named House and Senate committees on activities funded under the section and subchapter IV; the paragraph (5) five-year plan is published in the Federal Register, not submitted to Congress. The two congressional duties have different reporting officials, subjects, and deadlines, so they count separately, yielding 2.

Provision (a) requires an annual report on progress and implementation of specified technology transfer programs, submitted as part of the updated technology transfer execution plan. Provision (b) requires a separate evaluation, due within 3 years of enactment and every 3 years thereafter, assessing program success against short- and long-term metrics. Although both go from the Secretary of Energy to the same two committees and concern overlapping programs, they have different subjects (progress/implementation reporting vs. success evaluation), different deliverables, and independent deadlines/recurrence cycles (annual vs. triennial). Therefore they count as two distinct congressional reporting duties.

Provision [1] is the full section and states three separate duties to the designated congressional committees: (a) notice at least 15 days before any formal debt-relief negotiation (State and Treasury), (b) transmittal of the text of any debt-relief agreement with a justification at least 30 days before entry into force (State), and (c) an annual consolidated statement of budgetary implications due February 1 each year. Subsection (d) is only a definition and adds no duty. Provision [2] merely repeats subsection (c), so it adds nothing new. Total distinct duties: 3.

Both provisions describe the same annual report by the Social Media Working Group to the appropriate congressional committees; item [2] is merely one content element (paragraph (5)) of the report already listed in [1]. A report and its required contents count as a single duty.

Both provisions describe the same recurring biennial joint report by the Secretary of Defense and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff to the congressional defense committees on spectrum access implications; paragraph (2) merely specifies required contents of that same report. Provision [2] is a subset of [1], so there is one distinct duty.

Provision [1] (Pub. L. 117-263 \u00a7 1208) states one duty: an annual report by the Secretary of Defense within 90 days after the end of each of fiscal years 2023-2027 detailing assistance provided and its recipients. The listed subject matter of the program in subsection (a) is not a separate duty. Provision [2] (Pub. L. 117-81 \u00a7 1206) states two duties in subsection (c): (i) an initial report, due 180 days after enactment, on the security cooperation strategy developed for each covered combatant command, and (ii) subsequent annual reports (FY2023-FY2027, submitted concurrently with the section 386(a) report) on the implementation of that strategy. These have different subjects (the strategy itself versus its implementation) and independent deadlines/triggers, so they count separately rather than as a single duty with a recurrence. The strategy 'Elements' list in subsection (b) and the definitions add no separate congressional duty. Total: 1 + 2 = 3.

Provision [1] states one duty: submission of the information technology strategy to the appropriate congressional committees, with the accompanying annual consultation on implementation progress treated as part of that same duty/recurrence. Provision [2] contains the policy-development requirement (no congressional duty) and the client satisfaction survey (internal), but paragraph (3) imposes a separate duty to submit a summary of each survey's findings to congressional committees \u2014 a different subject, deadline, and recipient set from the strategy submission. Thus two distinct congressional reporting duties.

Provision [1] states one duty: an annual report by the Secretary of State on U.S. nationals believed unlawfully or wrongfully detained abroad, with its form and required contents (paragraph (2) merely lists contents of the same report, so it is not separate). Provision [2] states a different duty: a report due within 90 days after the end of each fiscal year to the Foreign Relations/Foreign Affairs and Appropriations Committees describing expenditures and support provided under subsection (d), plus envoy visits. It has a different subject, different recipients, and an independent deadline, so it counts separately. Total: 2 distinct duties.

Provision [1] is the full section containing two duties: (a) the Institute President's annual report to Congress and the Board on the Institute's status, and (b) the Board's budget proposal to Congress due by April 1 each year. These have different reporting entities, subjects, and deadlines, so they are separate. Provision [2] simply restates subsection (b), the budget proposal duty already counted, and its paragraphs (2)-(3) merely set the deadline/content and an instruction to Congress, adding no new duty. Total distinct duties: 2.

Both provisions concern the single report on the quadrennial quality of life review submitted to the Senate and House Armed Services Committees. Provision [2] is merely the deadline subdivision of the same duty stated in [1](d)(1), and the review/content requirements are part of that one report. Therefore there is one distinct congressional reporting duty.

Provision [1] states two separate duties: (iii) a one-time report describing the results of the EPSCoR effectiveness assessment, due 6 years after January 1, 2021, to specified Senate and House committees; and (iv) a recurring annual report at the end of each fiscal year, to a partly different set of committees, with a different subject (expenditures, awards, advisory committee representation). The assessment contract itself (i) is not a duty to Congress. Provision [2] states two further duties: a comprehensive facility plan submitted to Congress within 1 year of October 24, 1992, and annual reports to Congress on accomplishments, conformance to schedules, commitments, and expenditures, which is a recurring submission with its own subject independent of the one-time plan. Paragraph (1) (develop a least cost strategy) imposes no reporting duty. Total: 4 distinct duties.

Provision [2] is simply subsection (c)(2) repeated from within provision [1], so its annual report to the House Education and Workforce Committee and Senate Judiciary Committee counts only once. Within [1], paragraph (c)(1) separately requires the Council to make recommendations to the President and to Congress at least annually on coordination of policy, objectives, and priorities \u2014 a different reporting entity/subject and independent recurrence from the paragraph (2)(B) report by the members appointed under subsection (a)(2), which is expressly stated to be in addition to other reports. The (c)(1) internal review/report on Federal agency funds names no congressional recipient and adds nothing. Total: 2 distinct congressional reporting duties.

Provision [1] sets out three independent congressional reporting duties within subparagraph (B): (a) clause (v) requires reporting the nature of the threat and information retained to the congressional intelligence committees within 30 days when retention is extended to protect against an imminent threat to life; (b) clause (vi) requires annual reporting of access to information retained for technical assurance or compliance purposes; and (c) clause (vii) requires the head of the intelligence community element to provide a written certification (with specified contents) when retention beyond 5 years is approved for national security reasons. Each has a different trigger, subject, and timing, so they are separate duties. The certification's enumerated contents (I)-(IV) count as part of that single duty. Provision [2] is simply clause (vi) restated, duplicating a duty already counted, so it adds nothing. Total: 3 distinct duties.

Provision [1] establishes the annual presidential report on HIV/AIDS assistance implementation. The note in [2] does not create a new report; it merely directs that the same annual report required by section 104A(f) also be submitted to the Appropriations Committees, i.e., it adds recipients to the existing duty. Same report, same reporting entity, same deadline — one distinct duty.

Provision [1] contains two distinct duties: (a) an annual report by the President, due March 1 each year, on the legal and policy frameworks for use of military force (the listed matters in paragraph (2) are contents of that one report), and (b) a separate event-triggered notification due within 30 days of any change to those frameworks \u2014 a different trigger and independent deadline. Subsection (c) merely prescribes the form of the report and notices, and (d) is a definition, so neither adds a duty. Provision [2] is just subsection (c) repeated and states no new duty to Congress, contributing zero.

Provision (a) requires an annual December 1 report on the effectiveness of the official inspection and weighing system with legislative recommendations. Provision (c) requires a separate annual December 1 submission summarizing complaints from foreign purchasers of U.S. grain and their resolution. Although both are annual submissions by the Secretary to the same two committees, they have different subjects and are independent submissions, so they count as two distinct duties.

The full section states an annual report by the Ombudsman describing activities and effectiveness, submitted to the Secretary, Secretary of Education, and four named congressional committees \u2014 that is one duty (subsection (d)(1) and its submission clause (d)(2) are the same report). Separately, subsection (c)(4) requires the Ombudsman to make appropriate recommendations to the Director, Secretaries, and the same congressional committees; this is a different submission with a different subject and no tie to the annual report's deadline, so it counts as a second duty. The second excerpt is merely (c)(4) repeated and adds nothing new. Other subsections (establishment, public information, complaint handling, memorandum of understanding, definitions) impose no duty to Congress.

Provision [1] contains two distinct congressional duties: (a) the subsection (f)(3) notification to the Armed Services Committees within 15 days of a notice that an in-person quarterly meeting failed to occur, and (b) the subsection (g) annual report (first due 1 year after enactment, annually for 5 years) on exchange program activities, effectiveness, and recommendations — its listed elements and form requirement count as part of that one duty. The internal reports from the Exchange Program Coordinator to the Secretary of Defense are not duties to Congress and count zero. Provision [2] contains one distinct duty: the annual report to the congressional defense committees on obligations and expenditures of the Defense Operational Resilience International Cooperation Pilot Program, with its deadline and elements counted as a single duty. Total: 3.

Provision [1] states one duty: an annual report by the operational energy working group to the congressional defense committees by February 1 each year; its listed contents and the unclassified-form/classified-annex requirement are part of that single report. Provision [2] mostly directs the Assistant Secretary to create and maintain an operational energy strategy (not itself a duty to Congress), but paragraph (4) imposes a separate submission duty: transmitting the strategy to the congressional defense committees within 30 days of the FY2024 budget submission and every five years thereafter. That is a different subject, different reporting entity, and independent deadline from the working group's annual report, so it counts separately. Total: 2 distinct duties.

Provision [1] imposes an annual reporting duty on the Commissioner of CBP (with GSA) identifying activities and agreements under subsections (a) and (b); the long list of recipient committees is a single report's distribution, not separate duties. Provision [2] imposes a separate biennial report by the Comptroller General evaluating fee and donation agreements and fees/donations received. These have different reporting entities, subjects, and deadlines, so they are two distinct duties.

Provision [1] is the full subsection (h), which contains two congressional submissions: (a) the annual report under paragraph (2) describing obligations/expenditures and including recommendations (its listed contents count as one duty), and (b) the estimates of anticipated wildfire suppression costs under paragraph (3), submitted to the relevant congressional committees on a recurring schedule (the multiple submission dates are one duty with a recurrence; the independent-review and methodology requirements add no separate congressional duty). Paragraph (1)'s general accounting/reporting consistent with National Fire Plan procedures is not a duty to Congress. Provision [2] is simply paragraph (3) standing alone, duplicating the cost-estimate duty already counted. Total distinct duties: 2.

Provision [1] establishes one duty: an annual detailed spending report to the appropriate committees of Congress on tribal public safety and justice programs, with its enumerated contents counting as part of that single duty. Provision [2] is a statutory note that, in section 3(b), imposes a separate duty on the designated Coordinator to submit a report to specified Senate and House committees on Federal coordination efforts, with listed contents \u2014 a different reporting entity, subject, and timing. The definitions and coordinator duties in the note otherwise create no congressional reporting duty. Thus two distinct duties.

[1] states a one-time transmittal to Congress of a list of unconstructed authorized projects that received no obligations in the prior 10 fiscal years 
transmitted within one year of Nov. 17, 1986 
 that is one duty. [2] is a content requirement (funds spent) for the lists in the separate comprehensive construction backlog and operation and maintenance report under subsection (b)(2)(A); contents do not count on their own, but they belong to a different, independently established submission with its own subject and schedule. So the two provisions together reflect two distinct duties.',

Excerpt [1] contains the full section text, whose only congressional reporting language is paragraph (5): (A) a recurring 180-day progress report to the House Energy and Commerce and Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committees on compliance with the section, and (B) submission to those same committees of all reports required to the Court or parties to the Bodman Consent Decree. These have different subjects and independent triggers/deadlines, so they count as two distinct duties. The remaining provisions of (m) (rulemaking notices, determinations, application to products) impose Federal Register/rulemaking obligations, not reports to Congress, and contribute zero. Excerpt [2] is simply paragraph (5)(B) restated, i.e., the same duty already counted, adding nothing new. Total: 2.

Provision [1] contains one congressional submission duty: paragraph (10)'s transition and succession plan, to be developed before December 1 of each presidential election year and made available to the congressional homeland security committees. The paragraph (11) requirement is reporting to GAO, not Congress (the Comptroller General's notification is incidental to removal of the high-risk designation, not a duty imposed on the Department), and the remaining paragraphs list management responsibilities with no congressional reporting. Provision [2] states a separate duty with a different subject, trigger, and recipient set: the Under Secretary for Management must provide vehicle fleet rescission recommendations to the House and Senate Appropriations and homeland security committees as part of the annual budget process when components fail to pursue optimal fleet size. These are distinct in subject and timing, so they count separately.

Both provisions describe the same report by the Secretary of the Interior due within 1 year of January 4, 2011, and every 5 years thereafter, to the same committees. The second excerpt is merely paragraph (2), a content element of that single report, repeating the parent lead-in. A report and its required contents count as one duty.

Both provisions state the same reporting duty: subsection (d) requires the Secretary to submit a report on activities under the section to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and Senate HELP Committee within 180 days of June 12, 2002, and periodically thereafter. Provision [1] is the full section that contains subsection (d), and provision [2] is that same subsection quoted alone. The initial deadline plus periodic recurrence counts as one duty, and the other subsections impose program/evaluation obligations rather than separate congressional reporting duties.

Provision [1] states one duty: a biennial report by the Secretary (via the President) summarizing administration of the chapter, with its 13 required content items counted as part of that single report. Provision [2] states a separate duty: a report to Congress conveying the results of the review of other Federal programs under paragraph (1), with recommendations to resolve conflicts among Federal laws affecting coastal resources. Different subject matter and independent timing, so it counts separately.

Provision [1] establishes a single reporting duty: the Architect of the Capitol's semiannual compilation and report of expenditures submitted to the Senate and House, with the enumerated items (1)-(3) merely specifying required contents of that one report, and the recurrence being part of the same duty. Provision [2] is a note stating that this reporting requirement was terminated effective May 15, 2000; it creates no new or separate duty to Congress and therefore contributes zero. Total: one distinct duty.

Both provisions state the same single reporting duty: the Commission's annual report to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee describing waivers granted under subsection (c)(4)(A). Provision [2] is simply subsection (c) of the full section in [1], repeating that same duty, so it counts once. No other duty to Congress appears.

Both provisions state the same single duty: the annual research report under subsection (b), submitted by the University and NTID to the Secretary and the two congressional committees by January 10 each year. Provision [1] is the full section including subsection (a) (which imposes a priority-setting duty, not a reporting duty to Congress) and provision [2] is just that same subsection (b). The enumerated contents are part of the one report, so the total is one distinct duty.

Provision [1] imposes one duty: the Secretary must identify and report annually to Congress, at the time of the President's budget submission, the amount and location of National Forest System lands needing reforestation or not growing at potential, including the certification results of treated lands (the certification is part of that same report, not a separate submission). Provision [2] is a separate statutory note (Pub. L. 117-58 
s 70303) creating an independent duty: a report due not later than 1 year after enactment and annually thereafter, to specified House and Senate committees, on reforestation compliance and acreage; its four listed items are contents of that one report. The two duties have different deadlines, different recipients, and different subject scope, so they count separately: 2 distinct duties.

Provision [1] establishes an annual comprehensive report by the Secretary to the Veterans' Affairs Committees on the Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers, with subparagraphs (A)-(C) merely specifying required contents, data disaggregation, and privacy handling for that single report. Provision [2] is a separate statutory note (Pub. L. 111-163 
s 101(c)) requiring a different annual report 
u an evaluation of the implementation of section 1720G as a whole, covering both the family caregiver program and the general caregiver support services program, with its own independent deadline (not later than 2 years after a specified date and annually thereafter). Although both go to the same committees and overlap in subject matter, they are distinct submissions with separate authorities, scopes, and deadlines, so they count as two duties.

Provision [2] is simply the subdivision quoted within [1]. Both state the same requirement: budget material submitted to Congress must identify military housing projects proposed for lease contracts. Paragraph (1) of [1] merely grants leasing authority and imposes no reporting duty. Therefore the two provisions together state a single distinct congressional submission requirement.
